newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila frets over prices after devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Manila frets over prices after devaluation.

text.p: The prospect of rising inflation after last week's de facto devaluation of the Philippine peso has the government so worried that a hotline has been set up for citizens to report profiteers.
The government has also sent hundreds of inspectors around the country this week to make sure businesses are not using the currency turmoil as an opportunity to push up prices.
Officials at the Department of Trade and Industry told reporters on Friday that inspectors had checked 490 shops in the capital Manila.
Among shops that had broken pricing and fair trade laws was a dried fish stall, they said. The owner faces a fine and possible closure.

The peso has fallen close to 12 percent since the government last week decided to let the peso trade in a wider range, effectively devaluing the currency although it has started to stabilise. The peso was trading at 28.280 to the dollar on Friday afternoon.

The move came amid speculative attacks on currencies throughout Southeast Asia in the past few weeks. The government has established a formula for retail prices of essential commodities, through which it also can determine how much a price must rise as a result of a given depreciation in the peso. Businesses have been forbidden from raising prices any higher.
Besides threatening to punish "opportunistic merchants," the government is encouraging citizens to snoop and has publicised phone numbers to call to report any excessive price rises.
So far, prices appear to have remained stable but the worry is how long they will remain so.
The government says it will be able to meet a target set by the International Monetary Fund of 6-7 percent inflation this year. Inflation was under five percent in the first half of the year.
But since the peso's depreciation, businessmen have been calculating to see how much they should raise prices.
"In so far as our company is concerned, I don't know how many days we can afford (not to raise prices)," a senior executive at one of Manila's three oil refiners said.
"The goverment is using strong moral suasion and Petron is very big on that. Unless Petron moves, we cannot," he said.

Petron Corp, the country's largest oil refiner, was formerly a state-owned company and the government still has a stake in it. The smaller refiners dare not raise prices ahead of Petron as they would lose market share.
Automobile companies in the Philippines, which mainly assemble cars from imported parts, have said they will wait another week before raising prices.
The prospect of rising prices after the peso's fall has led to a series of curative suggestions from lawmakers.

Farmer-turned-legislator Jose Zubiri has urged that the nation give priority to achieving self-sufficiency in food production. "This is the only way ... to protect our people from the adversities of a volatile exchange rate."
Senator Raul Roco, one of the candidates for next May's presidential election, said people who gained from depreciation should be taxed and the money given to those who are losing out.
"The idea is that those who gained extra profit without any extra sweat, should help those who are disadvantaged by the depreciation."
Roco said he would propose this to the legislature when it meets again on July 28.
